categories: [Backend, Interactive]
image: figs/vegalite.png

```{r}
#| include: false
source("_helper.R")
library(vellumwidget)
```

[Vega-Lite](https://vega.github.io/vega-lite/) is the most widely used
grammar of graphics written as data: a chart is a JSON document with a mark,
encodings and scales. There are thousands of Vega-Lite specs in notebooks,
dashboards and documentation, and language models write them readily. vellumplot
is a grammar of graphics too, and its plots [are specs](spec-as-data.qmd)
already, so moving between the two is a translation rather than a
reimplementation.

## A spec from the Vega-Lite gallery

This is the [simple bar chart](https://vega.github.io/vega-lite/examples/bar.html)
from the Vega-Lite examples, pasted unchanged. Its data is inline, so the JSON is
the whole chart.

```{r}
bar_spec <- '{
  "$schema": "https://vega.github.io/schema/vega-lite/v5.json",
  "description": "A simple bar chart with embedded data.",
  "data": {
    "values": [
      {"a": "A", "b": 28}, {"a": "B", "b": 55}, {"a": "C", "b": 43},
      {"a": "D", "b": 91}, {"a": "E", "b": 81}, {"a": "F", "b": 53},
      {"a": "G", "b": 19}, {"a": "H", "b": 87}, {"a": "I", "b": 52}
    ]
  },
  "mark": "bar",
  "encoding": {
    "x": {"field": "a", "type": "nominal", "axis": {"labelAngle": 0}},
    "y": {"field": "b", "type": "quantitative"}
  }
}'

bars <- spec_from_vegalite(bar_spec)
summary(bars)
```

`spec_from_vegalite()` returns an ordinary `PlotSpec`: one `mark_bar()` layer,
the inline values as its data, a discrete x and a continuous y. It renders like
any other plot.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-alt: "Bar chart of nine categories A to I with heights from 19 to 91, converted from the Vega-Lite simple bar chart example"
vg(bars |> labs(title = "The Vega-Lite simple bar chart, drawn by vellum"), "vegalite-bar")
```

## External data, supplied from R

Most real specs point at a file: `"data": {"url": "data/penguins.json"}`.
`spec_from_vegalite()` does not download it. Pass the table you already have as
`data =`, with the column names the spec uses. Here the Palmer Penguins get the
names of the [vega-datasets](https://github.com/vega/vega-datasets) copy, and
the spec is a scatter in the style of the Vega-Lite gallery.

The spec's `"scale": {"zero": false}` keeps both axes on the range of the data,
which is where vellum puts them anyway, and its `tooltip` channel becomes the
layer's `tooltip`, so hovering a point in the widget below names its island.
Anything the translation cannot carry over is reported, not dropped in silence.
The `href` channel, a link behind every point, has no vellumplot counterpart,
and the warning says so:

```{r}
#| warning: true
pen <- palmerpenguins::penguins
pen <- as.data.frame(pen[complete.cases(pen), ])
names(pen) <- c("Species", "Island", "Beak Length (mm)", "Beak Depth (mm)",
                "Flipper Length (mm)", "Body Mass (g)", "Sex", "Year")

scatter_spec <- '{
  "$schema": "https://vega.github.io/schema/vega-lite/v5.json",
  "data": {"url": "data/penguins.json"},
  "mark": "point",
  "encoding": {
    "x": {"field": "Flipper Length (mm)", "type": "quantitative", "scale": {"zero": false}},
    "y": {"field": "Body Mass (g)", "type": "quantitative", "scale": {"zero": false}},
    "color": {"field": "Species", "type": "nominal"},
    "shape": {"field": "Species", "type": "nominal"},
    "tooltip": {"field": "Island", "type": "nominal"},
    "href": {"value": "https://allisonhorst.github.io/palmerpenguins/"}
  }
}'

penguins <- spec_from_vegalite(scatter_spec, data = pen)
```

## Now it is a vellum plot

Once imported, the spec takes the rest of the grammar. Pipe on a theme and
labels, and it is a widget with one more call:

```{r}
penguins <- penguins |>
  labs(title = "Penguins, from a Vega-Lite spec") |>
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
#| include: false
render_plot(penguins, "figs/vegalite.png", dpi = 150)
```

```{r}
penguins |> as_widget(height = 400)
```

Hover a point for its island, click a species in the legend, drag to brush,
scroll to zoom. The widget hosts the scene vellum solved; no Vega runtime is
involved.

## The round trip

`spec_to_vegalite()` translates the other way, for handing a vellum plot to a
Vega-Lite tool. Inline data comes along as `values`:

```{r}
vl <- spec_to_vegalite(bars)
str(vl[c("mark", "encoding")], max.level = 3)
```

The penguins go back out with their tooltip, and with `"zero": false` on both
axes: vellum frames a scatter on its data, while Vega-Lite starts a
quantitative axis at zero unless told otherwise, so the export says so.

```{r}
str(spec_to_vegalite(penguins)$encoding[c("x", "y", "tooltip")])
```

The two grammars overlap for the common cases: marks, encodings, scale domains
and types, binning and counting, faceting, inline data and titles. Outside that
subset (polar coordinates, layer effects, patterns, statistical marks Vega-Lite
does not have), both directions report what they left out.

## Specs from a model

Because a Vega-Lite spec is just JSON, it is also what a language model will
often give you when asked for a chart. The import above is one way in. The other
is to let the model write vellumplot's own spec format directly:
`vplot_ask(prompt, data, responder)` sends the model the JSON schema, the real
column names from `spec_fields()` and your request, and validates what comes back
with `vplot_from_spec()`. `responder` is any function from payload to JSON, so it
can wrap any model API. The [agent specs page](agent-specs.qmd) walks through that
loop, including the MCP server that exposes it to agents.
